analysis.body:
# Grid Interconnection Snapshot: What AI Load Growth Looks Like in the Queues

Across five major US grid operators, 8,364 generation and storage projects totaling 1.33 million megawatts sit in interconnection queues as of early September 2026. ERCOT leads with 438,086 MW across 1,778 requests, followed by NYISO's 319,095 MW in 1,414 requests and MISO's 299,721 MW spanning 3,833 projects. These queues represent generation and storage waiting for grid connection studies or approval, not direct measurements of data center demand—but the composition reveals where electricity infrastructure is being built. Storage capacity across all queues totals 328,106 MW, a proxy for managing variable renewable output and load swings; gas generation accounts for 184,509 MW, suggesting continued reliance on fast-ramping fuel for grid stability as instantaneous demand becomes less predictable.

Commercial electricity sales across eight major states totaled 54,797 MWh in June 2026, with Texas dominating at 15,753 MWh but paying the lowest price at $8.66 per MWh, while California's 10,024 MWh cost $27.33 per MWh—a 3.15× premium. Data centers are billed in the commercial class and thus embedded in these figures, though they are not separately identified. The six-fold variance in pricing between Oregon ($10.59) and California reflects both transmission congestion and renewable penetration, creating radically different economics for compute placement across regions. Texas's combination of high volume and low cost explains concentrated AI infrastructure investment there, while California's premium pricing and queue composition—71,682 MW mostly in solar and storage—suggest a state betting on renewable-heavy architecture despite higher interconnection timelines.

The queue fuel mix tells a growth story: solar dominates new capacity at 277,751 MW across all operators, wind adds 169,242 MW, and storage reaches 328,106 MW when combined, yet gas still represents 184,509 MW of new requests. MISO and SPP queues are deepest by project count (3,833 and 1,074 respectively), indicating more granular development across the Midwest and south-central regions, while CAISO's smallest queue (265 projects) reflects California's maturity and constrained grid. Watch next whether the gas-to-storage ratio in new requests shifts, as that will signal whether grid planners expect AI load to stabilize or continue its volatile daily cycling.
